Pocketwell

A household application that brings coupons, a priced shopping list and the grocery budget together so that the planned total equals the amount paid, and that tracks ten staple prices from official statistics to support letters to elected representatives.

Visit the site ↗How to useEngineering record

Engineering recordFor technical reviewers

Designed and shipped a household savings app: relational model on libSQL, money arithmetic as pure functions shared by screens and the assistant, cached price providers, and an AI agent with hard spending caps that can only propose changes.

A user asks the assistant to trim the grocery budget. The gateway checks the per-user hourly limit and the daily and monthly spending caps, runs the model with a bounded number of tool steps, and the tools call the same pure budget functions the screens use. The result is stored as proposals that the user accepts one at a time; prices come from cached Kroger and BLS data, so no page waits on a provider.

Key engineering decisions

01

One arithmetic for UI and agent

Budget and savings maths live in pure functions in cents, so the assistant cannot compute a different total than the screen.

02

Agent proposes, user commits

The agent writes proposals, never data, which makes every AI change reviewable and reversible.

03

Caps in cents, enforced server side

Model cost is metered per call and capped per day and per month, so a bug or abuse cannot run up a bill.

Notes for reviewers

Limits and next stepsLive shelf prices cover one Kroger-family store; adding retailers means new provider adapters behind the same cache.
01

Problem statement

Coupons, shopping lists and household budgets live in three separate applications. Shoppers learn the real cost of a trip at the register, cash back is counted before it arrives, and when food prices rise households have no simple instrument for showing the effect to those who decide.

02

Contribution

Five views each perform one task. Home shows the grocery budget left for the month. Deals lists coupons and offers for the selected store, each with its source, size, limit, expiry and redemption method. List prices every item at that store, applies the best matching coupon and projects the remaining budget, and a trip mode follows the shopper through the aisles. Budget records spending and changes to the plan through a review step before anything is saved, and explains how each number is derived. The receipt settles the trip once, and cash back stays separate until it is received. A prices page tracks ten staples month by month from official data, explains who determines each cost and drafts a letter that the user sends personally.

03

Architecture

Next.js 16 and React 19 in TypeScript with Tailwind CSS, and Drizzle ORM on libSQL hosted by Turso. Store and price providers are cached so that no page waits on an external service. The assistant works through a single gateway with daily spending caps and can only propose changes, which the user accepts one at a time.

04

Method and data

Money is represented in whole cents, and the savings and budget arithmetic lives in pure functions called by both the screens and the assistant. Store locations come from a verified list for the demonstration area, the Kroger API and OpenStreetMap; prices come from the Kroger API and the Bureau of Labor Statistics Average Price Data.

05

Verification and limitations

233 unit tests and 14 browser tests run on phone and desktop profiles. The name is provisional. Stores and prices are real, while demonstration coupons are labelled as examples, and live shelf prices cover one Kroger-family store.
